title: TC2-25357
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated July 27, 2022, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Vietnam. He is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated July 27, 2022, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant fears that he will be arrested if he returns to Vietnam because he is a Hoa Hao practitioner. In 2017, after his mother fell ill, the Appellant was introduced to Hoa Hao. He became a member of the faith in XXXX 2017. The Appellant alleges that he practiced alone, but that twice monthly he would practice in a group. In XXXX 2018 he heard news of the arrest of six Hoa Hao followers and decided that he had to leave Vietnam. The Appellant travelled to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Japan looking for a place to practice Hoa Hao freely. In XXXX 2019, the Appellant came to Canada. In December 2020, the Appellant made a claim for refugee protection.
The Appellant has presented new evidence in the form of an affidavit1 and photographs.2 The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted

According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.4

The Appellant provides in his affidavit that subsequent to the RPD decision, on Sunday XXXX XXXX, 2022, he attended a special event of the Toronto Hoa Hao Buddhist group at the Armour Heights Community Centre celebrating Vu Lan day. The Appellant presented two photographs showing his attendance on XXXX XXXX, 2022.

The evidence is clearly that which arose after the RPD decision. It is new and credible on its face. It is also relevant as it pertains to the Appellant's identity as a Hoa Hao practitioner, a key element in the RPD decision. It is accepted as new evidence.

The Appellant has not requested an oral hearing. I do not find that the new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant or that accepting the new evidence would justify allowing or rejecting the claim for protection. Therefore, I have not convened an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5

The RPD determined that the Appellant is not a genuine Hoa Hao practitioner. The RPD also determined that the Appellant's delay in making his claim after arriving in Canada undermined the credibility of his assertion that he left Vietnam out of fear and a desire to practice Hoa Hao. The RPD found that in the alternative, the Appellant does not have a particular profile as a Hoa Hao follower that would bring him to the attention of the authorities in Vietnam.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of whether he is a genuine Hoa Hao practitioner. He submits that the RPD erred in its assessment with respect to why he did not make his claim in Canada earlier and its assessment of his supporting documents. The Appellant has also argued that the RPD disregarded and misapprehended evidence in concluding that he would not be at risk of persecution as a Hoa Hao practitioner in Vietnam. The RPD did err in regard to the Appellant's religious identity

I have conducted an independent assessment of the record and I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in finding that he is not a genuine Hoa Hao practitioner. The RPD was concerned that the Appellant's responses to questions of the practices and principles of his faith were not from genuine practice of the faith and that rather, he memorized these details.

The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony lacked knowledge and detail that would be expected of someone who practiced as long as the Appellant has. This is not reflected in the record. The objective evidence shows that Hoa Hao has four gratitudes: "you must be grateful to your ancestors, towards your country, towards Buddhism and Buddhists, and respectful towards humanity in general."6 The Appellant was able to answer questions put to him about the four gratitudes, he identified having respect for ancestors, your country, people, and Buddhists or monks.7 The RPD was wrong to find that the Appellant could only name three. It was also wrong to find his response was perfunctory and without details; he was asked what the four gratitudes are and he stated them; he was not asked to elaborate any further.

When he was asked by the RPD to tell him about his faith, the Appellant testified that it followed the pioneer of the religion, Huynh Phu So,8 and the holy book Sam Giang. The RPD cites objective evidence that adherents pray twice daily and are vegans at least four times a month. The Appellant testified that he prayed every day, in the morning and in the evening.9 He further testified that on the 14th, 15th, 29th, and 30th of every month he only ate vegetables and that because he lived in someone's house, he did not have an altar set up when he prayed. The Hoa Hao faith celebrates three days of festivals: May 18, which is the formation of the religion, November 25, which is the birthday of the grandmaster, and February 25, which is the day that the grandmaster disappeared.10 The Appellant readily identified these dates without any prompting. The record shows that the Appellant answered the questions that the RPD put to him about his faith, and he expanded when he was asked to.

The Appellant provided letters11 from his spouse and a friend, to which the RPD assigned limited probative value as they were found not to be helpful in overcoming the lack of credibility in the Appellant's testimony. Both attest that the Appellant is a Hoa Hao follower. His wife explains that the faith has had a positive impact on his life. I assign them some weight in establishing that the Appellant is a genuine follower. I have also considered the Appellant's new evidence and I am also assigning it some weight. The Appellant testified before the RPD that he was scheduled to attend at a Hoa Hao group on XXXX XXXX, 2022, a month after the RPD hearing. The Appellant swore in his affidavit that he did attend the Hoa Hao group gathering. There is no reason to doubt his statement and he provided accompanying corroborative photographs.
I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant is a genuine practitioner of the Hoa Hao faith. The Appellant's delay in claiming
I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's delay in claiming undermines the credibility of his allegation that he left Vietnam out of fear and a desire to practice Hoa Hao.

The Appellant states in his Basis of Claim (BOC) that his fears in Vietnam over his Hoa Hao faith became crystalized in XXXX 2018 when he heard the news of the sentence imposed on six Hoa Hao convicted of obstructing officials and disturbing public order. He then started to look for a country where he could practice his faith freely. He travelled to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Japan. After contacting a friend on social media, who informed him of the religious freedom enjoyed in Canada, the Appellant applied for a visitor visa and came to Canada in XXXX 2019. The Appellant did not make his claim until almost two years later in XXXX 2020, just after his friend informed him that he could do so.

The Appellant testified that he travelled to those countries in late 2018 because he wanted a place where he could stay and practice his religion.12 He further testified that when he inquired about making a refugee claim in Japan, a lawyer told him he could not do so, but he never researched the matter on his own. When the RPD asked the Appellant why he did not make his claim in Canada earlier, he replied that he was not aware that there was a refugee programme.13 He did not speak to a lawyer because he did not have money, and he did not conduct any research on the internet.

I do not accept the Appellant's explanation. As the RPD noted, the Appellant is university-educated, and he has also demonstrated that he is capable of using the internet; he searched Facebook for his friend in Canada and located her, and he conducted research on the difficulties that Hoa Hao face in Vietnam. The Appellant could have become aware of the Canadian refugee programme by a simple internet search that he was capable of, but he did not do so and only spoke to some members of the Vietnamese community.14

The Appellant argues that he was not aware of the existence of the asylum system in Canada. That may be so, but he made no effort to become aware of it. He travelled in late 2018 with the thought of immigrating to other countries, and he was told by his friend in Canada about the religious freedom he would enjoy in this country. It is not credible that he would not search out the refugee programme in Canada given his fear of return to Vietnam and given that he came to Canada with the express intent of remaining permanently to practice his faith.15 The Appellant faced the risk of removal to Vietnam once his status as a visitor in Canada expired after six months.

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in finding that he could have conducted a simple internet search to find out about refugee claims because it did not consider the language barrier. I do not agree. He did not testify that the reason he did not conduct an internet search was because of a language barrier. Further, the Appellant provided in his visitor visa application and in his generic application form for Canada that he could communicate in English.16 I draw a negative inference on the Appellant's allegation of fearing for his safety in Vietnam from his delay in claiming in Canada for almost two years. The Appellant can freely practice his religion in Vietnam
The Appellant submits that the RPD misapprehended the objective evidence and thus the decision cannot stand. After conducting an independent assessment, I find no error with the RPD determination.

The objective evidence shows that the constitution of Vietnam states that all people have freedom of belief and religion, but that the law provides for government control of religious practices.17 Hoa Hao is one of 38 government-recognized religions stemming from 16 religious traditions. It is the third most popular religion in the country.18 There are estimates that there may be up to eight million followers in Vietnam and officials estimate that 90 percent of the population follows some sort of faith tradition.19

I do not agree with the Appellant's submission that the latest NDP reveals that generally speaking, there is no freedom of religion in Vietnam. While I acknowledge that there is some evidence of Hoa Hao being harassed by authorities as cited by the Appellant,20 the evidence indicates that overall, where a Hoa Hao follower is practicing his faith at home or in a small group setting, is cooperating with local authorities, and they or their leaders are not involved in political issues, they are unlikely to face harassment from the authorities.21

I also note the objective evidence indicates that the Hoa Hao typically face a low risk of official discrimination and it is those who engage in anti-Government activities who face a higher risk.22 There is evidence that indicates that there have been instances where Hoa Hao, from unregistered sects, who have been politically active, have been harassed by the police and that members of unregistered religious organizations that get involved in local political issues have been subject to harassment, arrest, and detention.23

The Appellant cites the definition of official discrimination used in National Documentation Package (NDP) item 1.4 and states that it includes persecutory outcomes. However, the same report summarizes that, in general, members of officially recognized religions, which includes Hoa Hao, can practice their religion with minimal inference from the authorities, especially in large cities.24 While some unregistered groups may face some restrictions, this will vary by region, ethnicity, and any perceived or actual involvement in advocacy or political activism.25 There is nothing in the record to suggest that the Appellant has engaged in any political activities or that he is a member of an ethnic minority in Vietnam.

I acknowledge the new Response to Information Request (RIR) that the Appellant cites in support of his position that the Hoa Hao experience disruption of religious activities and difficulties with the authorities, but the RIR also states that followers of recognized religious organizations can practice their beliefs without significant interference and that it is those members of unregistered groups that are politically active that have been harassed.26 The reason for the harassment often has little to do with the religion of the group, but rather the perceived threat the group may pose.

The objective country evidence regarding individuals who practice Hoa Hao at home or in small groups and do not have any political or activist profile indicates that it is unlikely that the authorities would have any interest in them. I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the objective evidence supports that a person in the Appellant's circumstances could practice his religion freely in Vietnam

Overall, I find that the Appellant has not credibly established that he cannot freely practice his faith in Vietnam. I find that there is not a serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted if he returns to Vietnam, pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Vietnam, pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
